title: Pneumothorax: Spontaneous, Traumatic and Tension Emergency Pathway

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with suspected or confirmed pneumothorax in the emergency department (ED) or acute medical ward: recognition of tension pneumothorax and immediate decompression, choice between conservative, ambulatory, needle aspiration and chest drain management for spontaneous pneumothorax, trauma-related pneumothorax, when to seek surgical advice, and discharge advice. Uses the British Thoracic Society (BTS) 2023 pleural disease guideline and NICE NG39 (major trauma), with US product labels for local anaesthetic and analgesia. Not for iatrogenic pneumothorax after procedures, children, or pneumothorax in mechanically ventilated patients.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-20.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi pneumothorax guideline was found; the pathway follows the BTS 2023 guideline (United Kingdom) and NICE NG39.

The BTS 2023 guideline refers to the BTS Clinical Statement on Pleural Procedures for needle aspiration and chest drain technique; that statement was not opened, so drain size, insertion site and aspiration volume limits are not given here.

The BTS 2010 pneumothorax guideline (size cut-offs, high-flow oxygen advice, aspiration limits) could not be opened; BTS 2023 states size is no longer an indication for invasive management but it dictates whether a procedure can be done safely.
NICE NG39 covers trauma only; for tension pneumothorax in a non-trauma patient the same decompression principles are applied, which is an extension, not a statement in NG39.
Local anaesthetic dose is from the lidocaine label (maximum 4.5 mg/kg, generally not above 300 mg); BTS 2023 gives no lidocaine dose.

Analgesia other than intravenous paracetamol (oral paracetamol, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, opioids) was not sourced from BTS 2023, NICE NG39 or an opened label, so no dose is given for them.
Oxygen: BTS 2023 and NG39 give no oxygen target or flow for pneumothorax; an evidence mini-review states oxygen may speed resolution in patients who are not hypoxaemic, but no flow rate was found.
Typical adult observation ranges are not taken from the guidelines.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.

pathophysiology.summary: Pneumothorax is air in the pleural space; it is called spontaneous when there is no trauma or causative medical intervention (BTS 2023, Section Spontaneous pneumothorax: Introduction). Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) occurs without suspected lung disease, although most patients show emphysema-like change on computed tomography (CT) (BTS 2023, Section Definitions and treatment principles). Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (SSP) occurs in established lung disease such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD); patients over 50 years with a smoking history are also treated as SSP (BTS 2023, Section Definitions and treatment principles). Tension pneumothorax causes haemodynamic instability or severe respiratory compromise and needs immediate decompression (NICE NG39, Recommendations 1.4.1 and 1.4.2). An open pneumothorax (chest wall wound) can progress to tension (NICE NG39, Recommendation 1.3.7).

symptoms: Chest pain and breathlessness; minimal or no pain or breathlessness with no physiological compromise allows conservative management (BTS 2023, Summary of recommendations).

Haemoptysis, chest pain and breathlessness within 72 hours before or after menstruation in young women suggest catamenial pneumothorax (BTS 2023, Other areas of clinical importance: catamenial pneumothorax).
Severe breathlessness with distress suggests tension (NICE NG39, Recommendation 1.4.1).
physicalSigns: Haemodynamic instability (low blood pressure, tachycardia) in a patient with suspected pneumothorax (NICE NG39, Recommendation 1.3.4).
A chest wall wound sucking air (open pneumothorax) (NICE NG39, Recommendation 1.3.7).

Clinical assessment is used to diagnose pneumothorax for triage; a negative extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma (eFAST) does not exclude it (NICE NG39, Recommendations 1.3.1 and 1.3.3).
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability or severe respiratory compromise with suspected tension pneumothorax: decompress before imaging (NICE NG39, Recommendation 1.4.1).
Open chest wound: apply a simple occlusive dressing and watch for tension (NICE NG39, Recommendation 1.3.7).
Physiological compromise in secondary pneumothorax (BTS 2023, Section on surgical referral).
Bilateral pneumothorax (BTS 2023, Section on surgical referral).
Spontaneous haemothorax (BTS 2023, Section on surgical referral).
Pregnancy with breathlessness, fetal distress or a pneumothorax of 2 cm or more (BTS 2023, Other areas of clinical importance: pregnancy).
precipitants: Smoking and age over 50 years classify a patient as secondary spontaneous (BTS 2023, Section Definitions and treatment principles).
Underlying lung disease such as COPD (BTS 2023, Section Definitions and treatment principles).
Chest trauma, including penetrating injury (NICE NG39, Recommendations 1.3 and 1.4).
Endometriosis in catamenial pneumothorax (BTS 2023, Other areas of clinical importance: catamenial pneumothorax).
Pregnancy and labour (BTS 2023, Other areas of clinical importance: pregnancy).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: No suspected lung disease and under 50 years or non-smoker; conservative, ambulatory, needle aspiration or drain are all options (BTS 2023, Summary of recommendations).
Established lung disease or age over 50 with smoking history; higher risk, drain usually needed (BTS 2023, Section Definitions and treatment principles).
Haemodynamic instability or severe respiratory compromise; decompress before imaging (NICE NG39, Recommendation 1.4.1).
History of chest trauma or a chest wall wound; treat with occlusive dressing and observe for tension (NICE NG39, Recommendation 1.3.7).
Recurrent right-sided pneumothorax near menstruation with history of pelvic endometriosis (BTS 2023, Other areas of clinical importance).

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Hypotension, tachycardia, low oxygen saturation, severe respiratory distress
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Instability or severe compromise triggers immediate decompression (NICE NG39, Recommendations 1.3.4 and 1.4.1).
ruleIn.normalValue: Stable blood pressure and pulse; oxygen saturation 95% or higher in air (typical adult values)

clinicalManagement.title: Decompress suspected tension pneumothorax
actions: Do chest decompression before imaging only if haemodynamic instability or severe respiratory compromise is present (NICE NG39, Recommendation 1.4.1).
Use open thoracostomy followed by a chest drain; use needle decompression only if the expertise for thoracostomy is not available (NICE NG39, Recommendations 1.3.5 and 1.4.2).
Observe for recurrence of tension after decompression (NICE NG39, Recommendation 1.3.6).
For an open wound, cover with a simple occlusive dressing and observe for tension (NICE NG39, Recommendation 1.3.7).

clinicalManagement.title: Assess and image
actions: Assess clinically (airway, breathing, circulation) and record oxygen saturation, pulse and blood pressure (NICE NG39, Recommendation 1.3.1).
Do a chest X-ray; add eFAST or CT as set out in Investigations (NICE NG39, Recommendations 1.4.4 and 1.4.5).
Classify as primary or secondary spontaneous, or traumatic (BTS 2023, Section Definitions and treatment principles).

clinicalManagement.title: Choose management for spontaneous pneumothorax
actions: Offer conservative management for minimally symptomatic or asymptomatic primary pneumothorax of any size (BTS 2023, Question A1).
Consider ambulatory management where support and follow-up exist (BTS 2023, Question A1).
If neither is suitable, use needle aspiration or a chest drain; the drain is used mainly for patients with high-risk characteristics (BTS 2023, Definitions and treatment principles).
Discuss all options with the patient and choose the least invasive option that meets their priority (BTS 2023, Good practice points).

clinicalManagement.title: Perform the procedure with analgesia
actions: Give local anaesthetic by infiltration (see medicines) and give adequate analgesia before and after pleurodesis (BTS 2023, Good practice points).
Follow the BTS Clinical Statement on Pleural Procedures for technique (BTS 2023, Definitions and treatment principles).

clinicalManagement.title: Handle persistent leak, recurrence and pregnancy
actions: Seek thoracic surgical advice for persistent air leak after 5 to 7 days of drainage, failure to re-expand, second ipsilateral or first contralateral pneumothorax, bilateral pneumothorax, haemothorax, at-risk occupations or pregnancy (BTS 2023, surgical referral section).
Options for air leak include suction, larger-bore drain, blood patch or chemical pleurodesis, endobronchial valves or surgery (BTS 2023, Question A3).
In pregnancy observe if the mother is not breathless, there is no fetal distress and the pneumothorax is under 2 cm; otherwise aspirate or drain (BTS 2023, pregnancy section).

clinicalManagement.title: Discharge advice and follow-up
actions: Arrange respiratory physician follow-up and a chest X-ray after 2 to 4 weeks if managed by observation or needle aspiration (BTS 2023, Question A2 discussion).
Advise no commercial flights until full radiological resolution, then wait 7 days after the resolved X-ray (BTS 2023, Question A2 discussion).
Advise permanent avoidance of scuba diving unless definitive prevention such as surgical pleurectomy is done, and advise stopping smoking (BTS 2023, Question A2 discussion).

regimens.indication: Local anaesthesia for needle aspiration or chest drain insertion
regimens.dose: Infiltrate 1% (10 mg/mL) solution into the skin, subcutaneous tissue and down to the pleura; per-dose range 5 to 300 mg (0.5 to 30 mL of 1%) for percutaneous infiltration; maximum individual dose 4.5 mg/kg and generally not more than 300 mg (Lidocaine label, Section 2.2 dosing table and Section 2.6). Supplied as 1% in 2 mL, 5 mL and 30 mL vials; no dilution. Aspirate before each injection to avoid intravascular injection (Lidocaine label, Section 2.1).
regimens.frequency: Single administration before the procedure; repeated doses allowed within the maximum
adjustments: Use the lowest dose that gives anaesthesia in older, debilitated or acutely ill patients (Lidocaine label, Section 8.5).
Severe hepatic impairment: risk of toxicity because of reduced clearance (Lidocaine label, Section 5.8).
Repeated doses raise plasma levels (Lidocaine label, Section 5.1).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Signs of local anaesthetic toxicity: circumoral numbness, tinnitus, tremor, seizures (Lidocaine label, Section 5.1).
Signs of methaemoglobinaemia: cyanosis (Lidocaine label, Section 5.2).
Oxygen saturation and pulse during the procedure (BTS 2023, Good practice points).
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to lidocaine or other amide-type local anaesthetics (Lidocaine label, Section 4).
Hypersensitivity to other components of the injection (Lidocaine label, Section 4).

regimens.indication: Pain from pneumothorax, chest drain or pleurodesis
regimens.patientGroup: Adults weighing 50 kg or more with pneumothorax pain
regimens.dose: 1000 mg intravenously every 6 hours (or 650 mg every 4 hours); maximum single dose 1000 mg and maximum 4000 mg in 24 hours; minimum 4 hours between doses. Supplied as 1000 mg in 100 mL (10 mg/mL), no dilution for the full dose. Under 50 kg: 15 mg/kg every 6 hours, maximum 75 mg/kg per day (Ofirmev label, Section 2.2 and Section 2.5).
regimens.duration: Until oral analgesia is possible or pain settles
adjustments: Severe hepatic impairment or severe active liver disease: contraindicated (Ofirmev label, Section 4).
Caution in hepatic impairment, alcoholism, chronic malnutrition, severe hypovolaemia or severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance 30 mL/min or less) (Ofirmev label, Section 5).
Count all paracetamol from every product against the daily maximum (Ofirmev label, Section 5.1).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Total daily paracetamol dose (Ofirmev label, Section 5.1).
Liver function in at-risk patients (Ofirmev label, Section 5).
contraindications: Severe hepatic impairment or severe active liver disease (Ofirmev label, Section 4).
Hypersensitivity to acetaminophen or any component (Ofirmev label, Section 4).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Minimally symptomatic (no significant pain or breathlessness and no physiological compromise) or asymptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax, regardless of size (BTS 2023, Summary of recommendations, Question A1; conditional by consensus).
Primary spontaneous pneumothorax in adults with good support, in centres with expertise and follow-up facilities (BTS 2023, Summary of recommendations, Question A1; conditional).
Primary spontaneous pneumothorax not suitable for conservative or ambulatory management (BTS 2023, Summary of recommendations, Question A1; conditional).
Suspected tension pneumothorax with haemodynamic instability or severe respiratory compromise; do not wait for imaging (NICE NG39, Recommendations 1.3.4 and 1.4.1).

Tension at first presentation; second ipsilateral or first contralateral pneumothorax; bilateral; persistent air leak after 5 to 7 days of drainage or failure to re-expand; haemothorax; at-risk occupation; pregnancy (BTS 2023, Section on surgical referral).

teaching.scope: Adults with suspected or confirmed pneumothorax in the emergency department (ED) or acute medical ward: recognition of tension pneumothorax and immediate decompression, choice between conservative, ambulatory, needle aspiration and chest drain management for spontaneous pneumothorax, trauma-related pneumothorax, when to seek surgical advice, and discharge advice. Uses the British Thoracic Society (BTS) 2023 pleural disease guideline and NICE NG39 (major trauma), with US product labels for local anaesthetic and analgesia. Not for iatrogenic pneumothorax after procedures, children, or pneumothorax in mechanically ventilated patients.
learningObjectives: Recognise tension pneumothorax and decompress before imaging when unstable.
Choose conservative, ambulatory, aspiration or drain management for spontaneous pneumothorax.
Know the indications for surgical advice.
Give correct discharge, flying and diving advice.
pitfalls: Delaying decompression for imaging in an unstable patient.
Inserting a drain without adequate analgesia.
Giving lidocaine above 4.5 mg/kg or 300 mg.
Allowing flights before radiological resolution plus 7 days.
keyPoints: Do not wait for a chest X-ray in a patient with tension physiology.
Size is no longer an indication for invasive management in BTS 2023.
A negative eFAST does not exclude pneumothorax.
Permanent avoidance of scuba diving unless definitive prevention.

patientEducation: A pneumothorax is air between the lung and the chest wall; many small ones settle on their own.
Return urgently for worsening breathlessness, chest pain or dizziness.
Do not fly until your doctor confirms the X-ray is clear and 7 days have passed.
Do not scuba dive; stop smoking to lower the chance of recurrence.
mdtReferrals: Emergency physician; respiratory physician; thoracic surgeon; radiologist; nursing team for drain care; pharmacist.
dischargeCriteria: Breathing comfortable at rest; X-ray stable or improving; drain removed or ambulatory device explained; return advice given; follow-up chest X-ray in 2 to 4 weeks and respiratory clinic booked (BTS 2023, Question A2 discussion).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Respiratory clinic and chest X-ray at 2 to 4 weeks; refer for surgical advice at second ipsilateral or first contralateral pneumothorax; flying 7 days after documented resolution; permanent diving avoidance (BTS 2023, Question A2 discussion and surgical referral section).
